sense.text:
“My son, prove thy soul in thy life, and see what is evil for it, and give not that unto it.” This part of the chapter goes into things a man may count good for himself that are not good for him, the meats and the dainties and the overeating. But that short part of the verse covers everything: you have to examine what is evil for your life and abstain from it, and not give yourself over to it.

It is not only food. It is the company you keep, the things you watch, the things you entertain and give ear to. Every one of them has to be examined: what is going to cause me to risk it all? Is this worth losing it all for, because my soul desires it or my flesh lusts after it?

Proving thy soul is taking moral inventory, as the Bishop taught: see what is evil for you, and don't give yourself over to it.

“For all things are not profitable for all men.” What may be good for one brother is definitely not good for another, and what is good for one sister is not good for another sister. You have to know yourself, to see what is beneficial or detrimental to your own life.

“Know ye not that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God?” Save this and hold on to it: the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom. The list that follows, fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, the effeminate, abusers of themselves with mankind (that is sodomy), are sins we are all familiar with, and every one of them is unrighteousness.

In among the thieves, the covetous, the drunkards and the extortioners stand the “revilers”. A reviler is a person who uses cruel, insulting or abusive language to attack the character or reputation of someone else.

That is where bitterness leads. Bitterness is intense animosity: a strong feeling of dislike or hatred, ill will or resentment tending toward active hostility, open aggression toward a person or a group. It goes from a thought to an action. Someone may have done something to you, and maybe they did; but holding that feeling, you stop being the victim and become the aggressor, instigating and starting things with that person, attacking with the mouth and at last about to put hands on somebody.

And the reviler is numbered with the unrighteous: “nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.”

Paul tells the Corinthians, “I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not”. Whatever spirit they expected him to come in, that is not the spirit he was coming in. They were constantly accusing Paul of things he was not doing, and Paul moved in the spirit of Christ: I don't know what you expected, but this is how I am moving.

He fears to find “debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults”. These debates are not in righteousness but in unrighteousness. A tumult is when the city is in an uproar, and the magistrates, the centurions, the police have to be called to calm it down.

“My God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already”: Paul will be sorrowful for those already in the midst of sin, the same sins read in the verse above and in 1 Corinthians 6. But here is the key: “and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed.” They did not repent.

There are things every one of us battles with, things we must fix and improve on. But for the Lord to give that assistance, there must be repentance involved. Everybody says that is a given; everybody does not know it.

Paul names two sins here, the fornication and the lasciviousness, but in 1 Corinthians 6 they stood with the extortion, the thefts and the reviling, all together and all unrighteousness. Some things Paul expounds on and others he keeps short. Some of the Corinthians would not repent of the transgressions they committed.

precepts.why:
Read straight on: “This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” Paul has dealt with this matter with them on numerous occasions. “I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned”: he is still dealing with those that sinned and did not repent.

“And to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare.” If he has to come to them again about the same lasciviousness, the same fornication, all the manner of sin he listed, he is not going to spare. Sometimes Israel has to be dealt with that way, because when you are too lighthearted or light-handed, they take kindness for weakness. Moses was the meekest man, and still they tried to overthrow him in the wilderness. So there were times when Moses and others of our forefathers had to deal more harshly and directly with Israel, as Paul is dealing here.

“Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness”: were he present, he would use sharpness, he would be fierce, “according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction.” The correction is to build them up, not to destroy them.

Why would Paul have to come that way? Chapter by chapter he had pointed out their sins: not keeping company with a fornicator, lasciviousness and all manner of sexual sins, the extortions, the reviling. And “his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful”. The they is the church of Corinth, the elders and scribes and Pharisees there. Paul's epistles are heavy, absolutely powerful; “but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.”

The Corinthians were talking junk: your letters are deep, Paul, but I have seen you, and I could whoop you. If he corrects me one more time, he is going to catch these hands. They hated the correction. But who appointed Paul over them? Christ did.

When he was there, they were not doing all that; once he was absent, they talked. Paul always got reports, from the apostles he left behind and from the house of Chloe, of what was being said and pushed in the congregation, and he wrote his letters according to it. So he answers: “Let such an one think this, that, such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such will we be also in deed when we are present.” Paul stood on business. Everything he wrote would be performed when he came, not sugarcoated, not changed. As soon as he hops out of the chariot, it is on sight.

That is where the building blocks of bitterness show: a church being corrected for the sins they are in, by the word of God, by the revelation of Christ, and wanting to put hands on the man who corrects them.

“After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth”: Paul was in Corinth, and his epistles were to the same people he dealt with there. That is why he could write, if I come again: he had already visited them. “Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house; and many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized.” Many of the Corinthians believed, not all.

Why did Paul deal with the Corinthians so boldly? “Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace”. Why be not afraid? Because of what the Corinthians were threatening to do. The Lord had to tell him: make your face harder than their face and your forehead stronger than their forehead, because they are going to try to sway you and intimidate you from teaching the gospel of Christ. Hold not thy peace means don't hold back, don't spare. That is why Paul wrote, if I come again, I will not spare: the Lord told him not to hold back, because the Lord knew the Corinthians were wicked.

“For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee”: Paul was bold because God had him. Talk your junk all you want; God got me. “For I have much people in this city”: many of those Corinthians who had not repented would repent, and the Lord gave Paul that confirmation ahead of the ministry. So “he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.”

Then “the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat”, and “all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things.” That is the progression of bitterness: from speaking evil, talking junk in 2 Corinthians 10, to putting hands on people. The Thessalonians dealt the same way. It was an uphill battle for the apostles, just as it is an uphill battle today for the prophets in the street teaching God's people. Our people grow a level of bitterness behind correction.

“He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck.” The same correction given to the church of Corinth caused some of them to grow hardened, bitter behind the correction. So some of the building blocks of bitterness stem from the hatred of correction, like a stubborn little child: why they got to point out my stuff? Why can't I do what I want to do?

But doing what you wanted to do did not work out too well out there: broken homes, broken minds, some needing medication, some self-medicating, looking for some kind of relief anywhere. To be reproved often, you have to be doing some sin or transgression often. And the remedy is not, stop correcting me. You are not mad at yourself for repeatedly committing the sin; you are mad at the one who repeatedly has to correct you for it. That makes no sense. But to the mind led by the flesh, by the desires of the soul, it makes perfect sense.

sense.text:
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword”, sharper than any sword we can manufacture, see or purchase, “piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit”. And it “is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart”: the word of God causes discernment. It shows where your thoughts lie, godly or wicked, and what your intentions really are. That is why your actions have to be lined up with the word of God.

You have to know a counselor's intentions: a lustful man asked about a sister and marriage will not counsel for your benefit but for himself, and a thief asked how to manage your money will not counsel you well. The word of God gives you that same ability about yourself. We are experts at using the word of God to discern the thoughts and intents of somebody else; but when it is ourselves, it is extremely difficult. Hence the topic.

Bitterness does not travel alone. It is not the lonely traveler, the only transgression you are dealing with. There are other contributing factors, other rebelliousness within you, and the bitterness is just the icing on the cake.

“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.” Bitterness builds not only between brother and brother or sister and sister, but within a marriage, between the spouses. In the household you will justify yourself, thinking that is the way it is supposed to be, never repenting of the bitterness you hold for your spouse.

So yes, sisters, this is something the Lord shows the men will have to repent of; and the same hatred is written of the wife. That is what bitterness really is: hatred. There will be hatred in that household that one of you or both of you will have to repent of. There is bitterness within the household, bitterness outside it, and bitterness within the congregation.

“Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart”. Two things are highlighted out of these two verses: the hatred and the grudging. The Lord says not to do it: don't have the hatred, don't grudge. When we do, that is the bitterness and the hatred among one another.

“Thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him”: you go to that person and let them know what the offense is.

“Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.” The Lord says, don't avenge, don't bear the grudge. That hatred and that grudging are the stark opposite of what God wants among his people, and that is the unity.

precepts.why:
“Endeavouring to keep the unity”. What does God want? God wants unity, and he wants you to work at it. That means there will have to be forgiveness involved, winking at ignorance involved, apologizing involved. For unity to abound you have to be able to do all of those things: forgive, forget, move on, get over it, whatever you want to call it.

How does someone go from being active in the body, helpful in the body, helped by the body in various capacities, to going and sitting down with the SPLC, sitting down with the enemy? How do you go from one extreme to the other? Bitterness. There was hatred involved, envy involved, all of it coupled together, because bitterness is not a lonely traveler.

And when you will not endeavour to keep the unity, you are rebelling against God.

sense.text: Kish was “a man of Benjamin”, “a mighty man of power”, and his son Saul was “a choice young man, and a goodly”, higher than any of the people “from his shoulders and upward”. That is where the history of King Saul opens: chosen of God, and none goodlier than he.

“I will send thee a man out of the land of Benjamin, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines”. Saul was chosen to be a savior of God's people.

So God has chosen each of you mighty men to be the saviors of the nation of Israel in these last days. You are not here to be anything short of that; that is who you have been called to be. King Saul never fought a battle by himself, and all those men battling with him were saviors too.

Saul would meet “a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp, before them; and they shall prophesy”. They were already prophesying; that is what they do. It is the same today: a man is going about his day and sees a company of men, all of them prophesying.

“And the Spirit of the Lord will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them”. How does a man go from going to a tailgate, the movies, dinner, a ballgame, the train or the bus, to standing in purple with those same men? The Spirit of the Lord fell upon him. There is no instruction manual for becoming a prophet, the way these apologists go through our welcome home package trying to figure out how to learn what we know. It must come through the Spirit of the Lord.

When a man first sees and hears it, his thought is, I never knew this, this is some good stuff, how can I learn more; not, I am going to be that. Holding post, reading, giving out flyers, let alone teaching: that had to be by the Spirit of the Lord.

“And shalt be turned into another man.” All praises to the Most High for being turned into another man. Or were you? That is the question.
When these signs come, “do as occasion serve thee; for God is with thee.” God is with you.

What the Lord prophesied through Samuel now happens: “a company of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them.” And “when all that knew him beforetime saw that”, everyone who knew you before you got around the company of prophets, they said, “What is this that is come unto the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”

That is your big mama, your uncle, your friends: what happened to you? You have celebrated Christmas your entire life; you grew up in the Pentecostal church; who tricked you? He was the best on the football team, going to college to play ball; what happened to him? An old friend messages you: you with those guys in purple? I saw you in a video. And if they are not having that discussion, not standoffish with you, it is because you have not fully changed into another man. You are still in a changing process, which is okay, but you must fully change into another man.

“But who is their father?” Who raised you? “Therefore it became a proverb, Is Saul also among the prophets?” It became a saying among the people, the family and the friends.

Samuel tells Saul, “The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people, over Israel: now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord.” The Lord remembered what Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him “when he came up from Egypt”, and commanded: “utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” The Lord told King Saul to slaughter everything.
“And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.” Saul kept the king alive.

“What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears”? Saul answers that “the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed.” They spared the best of the best; I spared Agag, but everything else we did destroy. We almost did everything the Lord said.

“When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel”? The Lord sent him to destroy the Amalekites “until they be consumed”, all gone. “Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord”? King Saul had an issue with being obedient to the Lord, and God called that disobedience “evil in the sight of the Lord.”

“Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord”. Remember those in Corinth who sinned and repented not: was Saul's first answer a sign of godly sorrow? There was none involved. He says he brought Agag and destroyed the Amalekites, “But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen”. He put it on the people.

Samuel proves what Ecclesiasticus 7 warns: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?” Sometimes we say, for the multitude of my sacrifices the Lord will not remember my sins. Yes he does, because there is no repentance involved. The repentance is left out: you are not going to the Lord sorry for your sins, you are adding sins on top of sins.

“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” When someone refuses to listen, refuses to take the correction or the counsel, it is an evil thing to be disobedient. You may be sacrificing your time, your money, all of these things; but with transgressions compounding one upon another and no repentance for it, what is the point of it all?

“For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” Disobedience is rebellion. When the Lord says endeavour to keep the unity and you will not, you are rebelling against God. “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.” Nobody really wants to admit it or say it out loud, but that is what disobedience means: you have rejected the word of God.

“The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.” Now see the picture: Saul dealing with rebellion, disobedience, rejecting the Lord, putting forth the finger and playing the blame game, and then told that the Lord is choosing a neighbour of his, one better than he. That is how bitterness starts to build. You get removed from an office, someone else is put into it, and now you look at that person with an evil eye as though they took your job. It is a progression: something was already there, other things were built upon, and on top of it all comes the bitterness; then the hatred evolves, then it turns to malice and violence.

That neighbour was not yet raised up, so it sat in the back of Saul's mind, and he started looking at everybody. That is for the brothers who claim all leadership hates them, the whole congregation, every sister, every brother, nobody wants them to succeed. Shut up. That is the bitterness creeping in, looking for someone to put the full blame on; Satan is all in your mind and in your ear.

The word of God is quick and powerful and discerns the thoughts and intents of men, so every one of us has to make sure he is not rejecting the word of God, nor playing the blame game.

precepts.why:
“Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger”. The putting forth of the finger is blaming. King Saul blamed the people right after saying he kept Agag alive: blaming them for keeping the sheep and the best of the flocks, and taking no accountability for keeping Agag the Amalekite alive.

The Lord is not going to hear any of us until we stop playing the blame game. I am bitter against this person because they did this to me; I have hatred toward that person because of that. The Lord does not care about your reasoning or your justification, because every one of us will be judged according to our ways. The Lord sees how that person is treating you, and the same way he sees how you are reacting to that treatment. If you trust in the Lord, you will act according to how God commanded you to deal with that situation, and let the Lord deal with that person.

“Bind not one sin upon another; for in one thou shalt not be unpunished.” The topic is bitterness, but bitterness is compounded upon other sins: there are other sins already in place before bitterness. With Saul there was disobedience first, and the Bible calls disobedience to God an evil thing; then he began to justify himself, and the Lord will not hear you if you justify yourself. By the time the bitterness rolls in, you already had other sins you were supposed to be working on before the hatred spilled over. For even one sin there is a judgment; but covetousness brings forth hatred, brings forth adultery, murder, bitterness, one bound upon another.

“Say not, God will look upon the multitude of my oblations, and when I offer to the most high God, he will accept it.” Isn't that what Saul just did? The people kept the best of the sheep in order to sacrifice unto the Lord. Don't say that through the multitude of my oblations the Lord will not worry about the sins I am in the midst of. Even with all those sheep for a sacrifice, God still highlighted his disobedience; as Samuel answered him, “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?”

sense.text: This is the history of David and Goliath. Goliath presented himself forty days, coming out every day to call out Israel and talk, and none would answer him. Then David: “this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God.”

“The Lord that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” David is dropping a resume nobody knew about: he had been killing lions and bears on the low. You walk a dirt road and see a lion torn up on the side, a bear mangled, and David is sitting at the house in a bearskin coat he did not buy at the mall. Then Saul: “Go, and the Lord be with thee.”

“And Saul armed David”, giving him his armour; but David had not proved it, had not practised or trained in it. Just give me five smooth stones: “he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook”, and “his sling was in his hand”, and he drew near to the Philistine.
“Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.”
The stone “sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.” “So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone”, “but there was no sword in the hand of David.”

“David took the head of the Philistine, and brought it to Jerusalem”, paraded it through Jerusalem, “but he put his armour in his tent”, kept as a souvenir. David did a valiant act: he defeated the Philistine that so many were afraid of, then cut off his head.

Abner brought him before Saul “with the head of the Philistine in his hand”, that huge Philistine's head in his hand. “Whose son art thou, thou young man?” “I am the son of thy servant Jesse the Beth–lehemite.”

“The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David”. Think on it: the Lord told King Saul that a neighbour better than he was chosen. David steps on the scene and drops his resume, kills the Philistine everyone feared, and returns with his head in his hand. And now Jonathan, the king's son, son of the king the Lord rejected, is tight with the brother God says is better than his father.

“Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David”. A king's son wore the finest garments, tailored and paid for by the king, and now the king sees that clothing on the brother who killed the Philistine, whom everyone is praising; “even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.” It does not say so, but the sword could have been given to Jonathan by his father. See the progression of it.

“David went out whithersoever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely: and Saul set him over the men of war, and he was accepted in the sight of all the people, and also in the sight of Saul’s servants.” All the people accepted David; Saul's own son was knit, joined close to him; Saul's servants reverenced him. Not for benefit's sake, for David was not yet king: he was an honorable man, a mighty man, and they saw the wisdom in him. Everybody likes this man except you. Everybody likes and loves this sister except you.

“The women came out of all cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet king Saul”. As far as the eye can see, sisters dressed lovely, calling King Saul; he starts feeling himself: maybe the Lord didn't reject me, maybe I still got it. Then he hears the words: “Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” “And Saul was very wroth, and the saying displeased him”: 38 hot, as they say down south. The songs he was excited about angered him once he paid attention to the words.

“And what can he have more but the kingdom?” He has the praise of the people, the sisters, my servants, my own son; what is left to give him but the kingdom? Instead of considering what God had already told him through Samuel, that he was choosing a neighbour better than he, Saul would not own that he rejected God and God rejected him. See where that spirit can take you.

“And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” Now David is the problem. Saul is not the problem: not disobedient, not the one who rejected God, not in the rebellion that is as witchcraft and the stubbornness that is as idolatry. He addresses none of that; the problem is David. Those are the building blocks of bitterness: bitterness does not just come about. There are other things first.

“On the morrow”, the very next day after Saul looked on David with an evil eye, “the evil spirit from God came upon Saul”. And “David played with his hand, as at other times”: he had already played for him before. “And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice.”

Meditate on how quickly that hatred can progress. Brothers at camp, at the entryway of the projects, were teaching a man out of Leviticus 19 that we cannot have hatred for one another, and the man listening said, what about that right there? The teacher turned around and brothers were rolling in the grass fighting. The hatred built so much that shaming the ministry was easier than letting go of whatever odds they had. You are trying to show repentance to your people at camp, and you are the ones showing hatred for each other. That should never be named among us. It is an extremely shameful thing.

“And Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with him, and was departed from Saul.” Saul now realizes the Lord has left him, and who the Lord chose, better than he.

Saul rejected the Lord and was in the midst of idolatry and witchcraft. David was sent for Saul's benefit: he slew the very oppressor Saul had been raised up to save Israel from, and he served Saul humbly, going whithersoever Saul sent him. Saul could not see it. He had an evil eye toward David and attempted to kill him, but the Lord was so with David that he caused David to avoid him.

“Therefore Saul removed him from him, and made him his captain over a thousand”. In verse 5 Saul set David over all the men of war; now, because he knew the Lord was dealing with David and not with him anymore, he took him off that office and shrank the company David was over. Yet “David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the Lord was with him”, and “all Israel and Judah loved David”. Even though King Saul did evil, all the people still loved David.
“Her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the Lord’s battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him.”

“The king desireth not any dowry, but an hundred foreskins of the Philistines”. “But Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.” The bitterness got to the point where he set David up to be killed by what he thought an impossible task: since I can't seem to catch David, I will send him among the Philistines in hope that the Philistines kill him. Bitterness caused King Saul to plot.

“Saul became David’s enemy continually.” Not only an evil eye: his enemy, continually. And David “behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul; so that his name was much set by”: everyone made account of the name of David from that time forth.

precepts.why:
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts”, and among them “an evil eye”. Saul eyed David from that day forward: was it with the looks of righteousness, or with an evil eye? An evil eye. “All these evil things come from within, and defile the man.” That evil eye was defiling Saul even further, after the Lord had already rejected him.

Some will say, I don't battle with bitterness. Satan says, hold my cup. Wait till you get the new job offer, the promotion or the demotion, the transfer to another school, the transfer to Louisiana or Philly that only a fool wouldn't take. You uproot your family and go, and now you are in a different location with different spirits and different circumstances, wondering why you are troubled in spirit. Where some come from, they do not deal with each other the way we joke; not everyone plays the dozens, and some people fight behind the words you call jokes.

If it had not been for the Lord, we would all be as Sodom. Don't think that because you are not dealing with it right now, you never will. The bitterness is going to tempt you. Hatred is going to tempt you. Unforgiveness is going to tempt you.

“But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” His servants counselled him to seek out “a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.” And “when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.”

Saul was already battling some things in chapter 16: the Lord rejected him, and an evil spirit from the Lord had taken him. David did a good thing playing the music to make that spirit depart; Saul was refreshed and back in the spirit again. Now in chapter 18 he has an evil eye toward David, ready to do him harm, and that evil spirit returned, and the javelin was thrown at the very man who had played it away.

sense.text:
“Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David”. In the cave “Saul went in to cover his feet”. He was not sleeping: Saul was taking a dump, his trousers down at his ankles covering his feet. That is why the king was by himself; a king does not sleep alone, but he goes to do that by himself. And David and his men were in the sides of the cave.

The men of David said, “Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand”. “Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily”: close enough to cut off a piece of his robe without Saul knowing that he or his mighty men were even there. David was no regular man; the Lord made his feet like hinds' feet, to run upon walls and beat his enemies into dust.

“Thou art more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil.” When David showed him the piece of his robe, Saul looked and saw where it had been cut without his knowing: David could have killed him. Had the shoe been on the other foot, Saul would have killed David. “When the Lord had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not.” Saul acknowledges that David is more righteous than he.

From the roof of the king's house David “saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.” He inquired after her: “Bath–sheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite”. “And David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in unto him, and he lay with her”.

“Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.” King David plotted against Uriah, to have him killed in the battle: the same thing King Saul tried to do to him.

You may not be tempted by that bitterness now. Just wait. David is no longer on the run; he is back in his kingship, in his palace, in his rightful place, and that same spirit tempted him, through coveting his neighbour's house; and the covetousness compounded with hatred and bitterness. Did David think, when he was running from King Saul, that he would ever be dealing with the same thing? Everyone always thinks the Bishop's classes and the other classes are about everybody else. Well, which one is about you? Just give it time.

“thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei”, of the house of Saul, the tribe of Benjamin, and “he came forth, and cursed still as he came. And he cast stones at David”. He showed his hatred and disdain for David because the kingdom was translated over to him, blaming David for Saul's death, blaming him for everything: “Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial”. “The Lord hath delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom thy son”: Absalom hunting you, you deserve it, for all the bloodiness you did.

See how the spirit of bitterness goes from person to person to person, built up differently for each. For one, the first thing rolling in is envy, and it leads to hatred and bitterness later on. For another it is covetousness, as with David; for others, disobedience. But it has a beginning point, and there are building blocks upon it.

Abishai says, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head.” David is king, and his mighty men are ready to put the man to death, but he says, “let him curse, because the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David.” “Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now may this Benjamite do it?”

“It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day.” David is in his repentant state: let him curse me for the evil I did, and I pray the Lord will have mercy. This is why David was a man after the Lord's heart: he could acknowledge his errors, his faults, his shortcomings, his sins, and always go to the Lord asking for mercy.

Shimei went along the hillside above them “and cursed as he went, and threw stones at him, and cast dust.” David saw this as an opportunity to turn back to the Lord, repenting of what he did to Uriah.

Whether it was lust and covetousness that brought David to hatred, to putting that brother to death, or envy, jealousy and rebellion against God that drove Saul to try the same on David, everyone has his path. But the icing on the cake for everyone is bitterness.

“There is one that is wise and teacheth many, and yet is unprofitable to himself.” King David a prophet of God, King Saul chosen of God; yet at those moments, until the repentance came in, they were unprofitable to themselves, because they committed the transgressions. That is like all of us. Family and friends now ask, are you among the prophets? Your neighbour sees you walk to your car in your purple and gold: you with those guys? I saw them here, I saw them there.

You don't want to be the one God called with his wisdom who, through lack of application and of examining himself, is unprofitable to himself: beneficial to everyone who came his way, answering questions, casting down imaginations and everything that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, but when it is time for him to apply it, there is an issue.

Men in the ranks: your peer tells you something and you have a gripe with him, but when a captain says the same thing, right away you take it. Some call it respect of persons, respecting one rank or one leader over another, and it shows the bitterness is in a lot more of us than we want to admit. Satan is right at your door. If those other building blocks, which may seem like nothing to you, are already in place, all he needs is for the bitterness to become full-fledged and overflow. An order or a directive comes on your phone and you think, here we go, and Satan is right there: I bet he ain't asked nobody else to do it. Why they always asking you?

We stay in denial until the breach in the wall breaks and it overflows like Hurricane Katrina, and you ask, how did I end up here? You did not deal with it when it was little building blocks and nuances. You said nothing and acted like everything was normal.

precepts.why: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.” You can be a teacher, a preacher to others, an instructor in wisdom to others, and it be unprofitable to yourself. Paul, dealing with the Corinthians, did not want to be a castaway: not only did he have to teach it to them, he had to live it as well, or he would be, as Ecclesiasticus 37 says, unprofitable to himself. And we cannot have that.

sense.text: How do these building blocks get dismantled? “All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes”: the way we operate, the way we deal, so accustomed to saying nothing is wrong, I'm good. That is normalizing the bitterness, and it is not supposed to be so. “But the Lord weigheth the spirits”: the Lord knew what was going on within King Saul, knew what was going on within King David, and knows what is going on within each of us.

“Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.” As your thoughts and intentions are discerned by the word of God, God will establish your thought process and your intentions according to his word, if you commit your works unto the Lord and are not living a double life. The bitterness brewing and stirring within us, the hatred, the Lord will establish all of that if you commit yourself to the works.

“Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you”. The root of bitterness starts very small. “And thereby many be defiled”: not nobody in here, not any of you righteous brothers and sisters, but many. It is not what man says; God says many are defiled by that root of bitterness.

“Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself”. If there is an issue, instead of letting it spring up into bitterness, deal with that brother, or with that sister, one on one. Some will say, I don't want to do that; then let the bitterness spring up. This is the preventive measure, so as not to build upon it.

“And discover not a secret to another”: when there is an issue, everyone should not know about it before the person you have the issue with. How is it that everybody else knows, and the one it concerns knows nothing about it? That doesn't make sense. The Bible says go to that person one on one and deal with them.
“Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame”.

precepts.why:
“Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone”. What King Solomon wrote in Proverbs, the writings of wisdom, Christ says the same; and the Lord wrote it in the law, in Leviticus 19, not to bear grudge but to rebuke thy neighbour and not suffer sin upon him. That does not mean telling everybody else; you go to that person and let them know what the offense is. The law, the writings of wisdom and Christ himself all say the same thing: the way to keep your soul from being destroyed by bitterness.

“If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.” The objective of going to that person is to resolve it and to gain that brother, gain that sister, rekindle and gain that love in the marriage, as husbands are not to be bitter against their wives: to regain the brotherly love the Lord commanded us to endeavour to keep.

“But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more”, and if he neglects them, “tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.” Christ had to expound on it because some did not want to listen to the law and the prophets and go one to another. If you won't hear your brother out to gain your brother, you might need to be put out of the church, because you do not love your neighbour as yourself.

sense.text:
“Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice”. That bitterness, that hatred, will become physical at some point. How is there abuse in relationships? A man who assaults his wife, or a wife who assaults her husband, did not wake up that day saying, as soon as I open my eyes I'm going to beat the person sleeping next to me. Things compounded over time and were left unresolved: you never went to your spouse and talked them out, never laboured to gain them, to win your husband or your wife back over so that whatever spirit is on them would flee. That is how it gets to malice and to violence.

King Saul did not just throw that javelin; he did not wake up saying whoever comes in this room, I'm throwing a javelin at them. Things led up to it that he would not acknowledge and repent of. He was not sorrowful to God, so the Lord did not remove that spirit from him. There are times we have those spirits in our own houses and the Lord does not remove them, because there is a lack of accountability among us: we are still putting forth the finger.

So it goes deeper than how do I recognize bitterness and how do I deal with it. We have to deal with the things before the bitterness. Who are you bitter toward? Is it envy? Covetousness? Have you rejected God altogether, so that you don't believe? Nobody woke up this morning with the mind just to hate a brother or a sister. If you have that hatred, that bitterness, find what led up to it, and you will know what to fix. It is not just for the brother who asked the question; it is for all of us.

Read again before verse 5, as it was read earlier: Paul writes “to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare”. He has dealt with their sins before, and if he must come about the same things again, he will not spare them.

“For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God.” As they were learning the gospel of Christ, Paul affirms the power of God among them: how God raised up Jesus through his power, the same way he is going to do with us; “we shall live with him by the power of God toward you.”

“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” You have to prove your own self, as Ecclesiasticus said: prove thy soul in thy life, see what is good for it. The self-examination is very extensive. It holds up a mirror against yourself and takes that moral inventory.

If you now know that bitterness is your issue, first find out who you are bitter toward, and then why. What caused it? A promotion? A demotion? A removal? Is it envy? You might just be an envious person. You cannot get rid of the bitterness unless you deal with the other contributing factors.
